en: A General Discourse on the Nature and Mutual Correspondence of the Great Universal Offering for the Holy and the Profane, Beings of Land and Water, within the Dharma Realm: Volume One.
By the Practitioner of Pure Karma, Zhi Guan (Zheng Yingfang).
I prostrate to the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions, All of whom are those whose radiance shines everywhere.
Within this Sahā world, you manifest the Flower Treasury, With layers of bodies and lands intermingling in brilliant light.
I dare to pray that you will likewise, with great majestic power, Bestow your grace upon the foolish and ignorant, so they may achieve sage-like wisdom.
Not departing from the one true reality, phenomena and principle are revealed; saints and ordinary beings are unimpeded, all universally cool. The General Commentary states:

The fundamentally innate single mind manifests according to conditions. Sentient beings are bound by suffering, while the Buddhas manifest their bodies. There is nothing to be delivered, yet they deliver;
it remains as it is, equal and impartial—this is what is called the True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Within this single truth, there is radiance.
Pure and radiant is the oceanic assembly of the Avataṃsaka; clouds of offerings arise, and its brilliant splendor is ever-present at all times and in all places.

Those of inferior capacity do not believe, thereby isolating themselves from the true thread [of reality]. For those of great resolve, it is a single site of practice that encompasses the ten dharma realms.
Throughout the ten directions and ten periods of time, the inexhaustible and layered manifestations appear suddenly and perfectly within a single thought-moment.

Remaining unmoving and undispersed, where could they go, and where could they follow? To highlight this, the origin of Ānanda’s offering of food is presented; to highlight this, the origin of the *Jingzhu* (Pure Abode) repentance is presented;
to highlight this, the origin of Emperor Wu of Liang’s *Shuilu* (Water and Land) ritual is presented. All phenomena are fundamentally quiescent; when employed, they respond to all needs. Since...
It has no beginning and no end; its wondrousness is the ultimate natural state. It is neither eternal nor subject to annihilation. Its profound single flavor universally benefits all sentient beings.
From the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty onward, there have been those who practiced this Dharma. From the time of Zhipan onwards, the written records may be examined.

Master Nian drew upon these sources, and for the most part followed the ancient traditions; Master Hong further expounded upon them, with much that is suited to the present day. This is the "Hand and Eye" [of the lineage].

Though these forms differ, the underlying aspiration remains the same. At the site of the Kukkutārāma, a new altar has been established in the East; there, the banner of the Buddha-dharma is raised to serve as a guide for sentient beings.

Reflecting with deep sorrow upon our nation’s profound benevolence and generous grace, whose virtue extends to the boundless, one laments that the masses of people, due to the divergent karmic conditions of their past deeds, have given rise to such manifold varieties.
Consequently, the teachings of the Five Vehicles have all fallen into neglect, and the realms of the Seven Destinations...
My chronic ailment has suddenly flared up; my remaining exhaustion has not yet subsided, and my spirit finds no consolation.

Whenever I contemplate striving for myself to contribute to the Imperial Realm, I realize that although wholesome dharmas are many, none are as fundamental as those pertaining to water and land. Thus, relying upon the mirror of emptiness, I shall deeply analyze even the finest dust.
Without artifice or difficulty, I shall express my thoughts with a straightforward mind. With few worldly affairs to occupy me, my spirit and intellect will become clear. This is my humble petition.
It is not much; when mind and speech are free from falsehood, the One True Dharma Realm is not distant and can be reached. The various classes of awakened spirits will come to attend with equanimity.
Even a tiny contribution is of benefit, for names and forms are not empty. This very *Avataṃsaka* points the way back to the Ultimate Bliss.
Cultivating the mind is fundamental; employing the Dharma is what brings spiritual efficacy. Let the gentlemen of later generations not treat this with even the slightest casualness.

General Discussion: Outline of the Altar Diagrams, Volume Two:

The Commentary states: This is a general outline of the sequence for water and land [practices]. As for the remaining minor details, they should be understood from the text itself. Alas!

The characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are exquisite and naturally unobstructed; like a crystal pavilion, every section is transparent and pervasive. The single, solid, and dense body manifests within every single atom.
Wandering through the cycles of rebirth without returning is called "sentient beings" (*sattva*); they dwell within the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
It is eternally fresh, for the Dharmakāya is not subject to defilement. If one speaks of the Buddha saving sentient beings, it does not lie outside the wondrousness of the single mind.

Rituals at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) are themselves one's own cultivation. There must be those who, having realized the mind and attained Buddhahood, can then propagate its majestic spiritual power, so that all living beings within the Dharma-realm may, with a single thought, turn their light back upon themselves and return to what they originally possessed. Furthermore...

What leisure have we to attend to the host of the feast, to ostentatiously elaborate ritual protocols, to provide verbose expositions on the gates of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), or to perform empty recitations of sutras and repentance rites—thereby losing the essence while clinging to the form?
Observe how the phenomenal appearances of sentient beings largely obstruct the true mechanism;
for the most part, they are the same, and I leave them with a single sigh. What I now deliberate upon approaches the path of brevity. Yet, there is a singular radiance.

Circulating throughout the Dharma-realm, if you encounter one who knows this sound, there will surely be the opportunity to grasp it. The turbulent waves of the sea of suffering will, from this moment on, cease in a single breath;
boundless Dharma-joy is neither of self nor of another. I hope each of you will humbly empty your minds and seek true salvation with depth.

This is acceptable. Regarding the current discussion of the fundamental texts: those that preserve the essential points follow the original wording (referring to the three great masters Zhipan, Lianchi, and Hongyuan), while those that provide corrections and supplements incorporate new interpretations, as detailed in the subsequent text. Let the reader examine this.
Volume Nine:
Iconographic Models and Eulogies, Part One:
The Square Altar. This is to be established within human dwellings as is appropriate.
However, it is also necessary that there be space outside the altar on all four sides to allow for circumambulation.
This second circular altar is established by taking ancient precedents as a standard for the present.
By dividing the two gates into upper and lower sections, its design becomes precise, clear, and well-discriminating, making it quite feasible to implement; yet, it must be done separately.
The altar pavilion has been constructed.

Following this, another great circular altar diagram is established; because the mind must be at ease regarding the ritual matters and because the measure is boundless, it is drawn by taking my own nature as the model.
When the power of mind and the opportune moment coincide, it is indeed possible to construct this Flower Adornment Pavilion. A mere snap of the fingers and the gates shall open;
do not harbor thoughts of difficulty or ease.
The treatise states: This pavilion is formed by ten pillars. On the left and right of each pillar is a seat, and these seats are all subtle.
It is oriented toward the interior. Between the two seating areas, there is one gate and one flight of steps; seven are discarded and three are used.

Each pillar has one banner, and between each pair of pillars is one lamp. On the back of each banner is a mirror; the mirrors are on the inner side of the pillars, while the banners are on the outer side of the pillars.
For the five central seats (the first, second, third, and the fourth, fifth, and twenty-fifth), lamps are placed on both the left and right sides, and mirrors are placed on both the front and back.
Ten lamps, ten lamps; ten mirrors, ten mirrors—these serve to symbolize the meaning of inexhaustible, layered profundity.
The pavilion is three *zhang* in diameter and nine *zhang* in circumference. The steps are seven feet above the ground. The eaves of the pavilion rise one *zhang* and four feet above the steps.
The distance between two pillars is nine feet; from the outer edge of a pillar to the eave is five feet. Within these five feet, excluding the interior...

Fifteen *chi* constitute half of the space outside the seating area. Excluding these fifteen *chi*, there is a veranda with a railing at the edge; the remaining two *chi* in the center are reserved for circumambulation.
The central steps are used exclusively for the passage of the true deities and spirits; the presiding official indicates their entry and exit by using the left and right stairs.
The gates of the left and right railings are locked by the officials in charge of incense and lamps; no other persons are permitted to enter.
The outline states: Having collected various texts concerning the Water and Land rites and discussed them, I have completed eight fascicles.
A guest who read them and harbored doubts raised a flurry of questions and objections; I answered each one in turn.
Question: "In a single thought-moment, one universally contemplates immeasurable kalpas; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding.
Thus one thoroughly understands the matters of the three periods of time and transcends all expedient means to achieve the Ten Powers.

Now, regarding the basis of this treatise, the eleven seats of the upper hall have been expanded to twelve seats by adding the holy sages of the Pure Land outside of the Buddhas and the Sangha. In reality, however, the Pure Land is...
This is but one among the infinite gateways of the *Avataṃsaka*; to arbitrarily increase or decrease it would surely not accord with the universal mind (*puxin*). Answer:

This is precisely the universal mind. For the sake of sentient beings throughout the ten directions, who since time immemorial have placed their faith in the Triple Gem in a general way but do not know how to specialize, and who have thus suffered in aimless wandering without attaining liberation—this [sūtra] now guides them toward a single Buddha-land.
Entering fully into the One, every Buddha manifests; this is precisely the conduct of the worthy. How could one worry that it is not universal?
Furthermore, what increase or decrease is there between ten and eleven? As the Sūtra says: "Within every single atom of all the Flower Treasury World, the Dharma-realm is seen;
jewel-radiance manifests Buddhas gathered like clouds. This is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field.

Question: Since the *Liang* Repentance is initiated and correctly initiated, cultivated and thoroughly cultivated, its merit rescues from all suffering and is revered as the fundamental principle of all places of practice (*dōjō*).
Why then have you now separately composed the *Fǎlún* Repentance? Will it not be able to evoke a universal resonance? Answer:
Although the *Liang* Repentance is excellent, those who perform its rites in the world mostly fall into mere routine; their mental nature remains [untransformed]. Furthermore—
Separated. How could the realm of phenomena ever be reached? Now, one who presides over the ritual must take solemn repentance as their primary responsibility.

If such a person is absent, then even if one merely performs rites at the outer altar, it will likewise be ineffective. Furthermore, the precepts, concentration, and wisdom of the Triple Gem are fully manifested within the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras;
to cultivate oneself through these and thereby trigger the latent causes of awakening, while invoking and prostrating before them, is precisely what is required.
I take refuge in the Teacher of all Buddhas. Indeed, the great suffering of body and mind arises solely from conditions;
if one can maintain a sincere and concentrated mind, repentance will bear fruit immediately. Since this essence permeates both sentient beings and Buddhas, it is a burden that can be shouldered;

it is not something easily demanded of the common worldlings. The suffering accumulated over kalpas has the three poisons as its root, yet delusion is the most difficult to shatter—reflecting upon this...
"All sentient beings are my kinsmen. How could I not seek the true light to shatter their darkness? The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"For example, suppose there is a person who is compassionate, filial, and fraternal. Having encountered worldly calamities, his parents, wife, children, brothers, and sisters have all been lost.
Suddenly, amidst the vast wilderness and upon the roads, they encounter one another. Looking up..."
I respectfully submit this response. My heart knows no satiety; I pray that those who practice the Dharma will deeply embody this intention.

May all sentient beings respond to this resonance and all know their way home. One must not merely recite the vast, ancient, and enduring vows of the sages—vows so arduous and sublime—and then perfunctorily prostrate oneself to fulfill a formal obligation, thereby betraying the spirit of this very place of practice.
[They are] external humans and devas.
Question: Generosity, precepts, patience, diligence, as well as meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, supernatural powers, and so forth—all such things are entirely sovereign.
This is the power of the Avataṃsaka Samādhi. Therefore, at the water and land ritual sites, by means of the seven locations and nine...
Question: These [assemblies] were established as fixed characteristics, yet now they are omitted. Why is this? Answer: To abandon the false and rely upon the true, the *Avataṃsaka* has appeared.
While the seven locations and nine assemblies discuss the fundamental school of the worthy ones, the Elder [Nāgārjuna] has already expanded them into ten locations and ten assemblies.

Regarding the fundamental principles of the current discourse, there are ten locations in total. The first location is within a single moment of mind (*ekakṣaṇacitta*), wherein all Buddhas and sentient beings are luminously unobstructed;
this is the realm of the pure, singular nature (*prakṛti-viśuddha-dharmadhātu*). The second location is the outer altar. The third location is the altar for dispatching messengers.
The fourth location is the pavilions in the void above the pure path. The fifth location is the bathing altar.
The sixth location is the Inner Altar. The seventh location is the Pure Land Altar. The eighth location is the Food Offering Altar.
The ninth location is the Flower Adornment Altar. The tenth location is the Universal Dispatching of the Sages to the Ten Directions.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like empty space; therein all Buddhas abide. Without going and without staying, they are seen everywhere.
Now, within a single thought-moment, the Buddhas born therein are observed simultaneously as the First Assembly.

Throughout the ten directions, more than seven thousand two hundred scrolls of Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and Dhāraṇīs were recited in advance; the radiance of the Dharma-treasure interlaced and reflected one another. As for...

The second assembly: at the summit of the outer altar, prostrating before the Dharma-wheel Jewel Repentance, emitting the light and sound of the Dharma from within the hearts of sentient beings constitutes the third assembly.
The impurity-tracing Vajra, the ten Great Vidyārājas, and the eight classes of devas and nāgas serve as witnesses to the boundary-binding constitutes the fourth assembly.
The Holy Avalokiteśvara, seated within the site of enlightenment, radiates light from between his eyebrows.
The Fifth Assembly: The Tathāgatas Vairocana of the ten directions sit in a circle around the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and emit light from between their eyebrows.

This constitutes the Sixth Assembly. When requesting [the Master] to ascend the hall, providing offerings for the ritual bathing and the midday meal, and praying for amnesty and pardon, this constitutes the Seventh Assembly.
The Dharma Master sits and preaches the Three Refuges and the Bodhisattva Precepts, opening the realm of the Buddha for all sentient beings.
The eighth assembly: ordinary and holy beings from the ten directions together attend the site of enlightenment to fully practice the methods of the *zhāi* (fasting/retreat). The ninth assembly:
having completed the escorting of the holy ones, he again manifests the ritual procedures for the *yogic* offering of food (*yogāhāra-vidhi*), delivering sentient beings without limit.
This constitutes the tenth assembly.
Question: "The vastness, magnificence, and beauty are all identical to empty space; they do not obstruct one another, nor is there any confusion.
In the past, the inner altar lasted only five days, and the offering of food likewise lasted only five days, each having its own proper measure. Why is it now all uniform?"
Answer: By means of seven [days]. In the oceans of lands throughout the ten directions, immeasurable and boundless Buddhas each manifest their spiritual powers within a single thought-moment.
Since the altar site has already been prepared for seven days, what hindrance could there be in having matters occurring during or outside those seven days?
First one sprinkles water for purification externally, and subsequently one establishes the boundary internally; this is not a matter of confusion.
Question: The sublime Dharma and its subtle sounds, through metaphors and corresponding syllables, and by the infinite spiritual powers of the Buddhas, have all entered my body.
Regarding the twelve divisions of the sūtras for the outer maṇḍala, which one ought to diligently recite, now none of these are being done.

To merely offer the single repentance of the Dharma Wheel—is this not too shallow? Furthermore, although the recitation of sūtras in former times was called a virtuous practice, yet as for the radiance...

[The practice] has become scattered; how can it be said to conform to a systematic scale? Answer: You are mistaken. This was originally not for the purpose of reciting scriptures, but for the purpose of examining the Tripitaka.
Since the practice of examining the Tripitaka could not be carried out, it was replaced by the recitation of scriptures, and consequently, both the Vinaya and the Śāstras were set aside.

Furthermore, the twelve divisions [of the canon] refer to the *geya*, *itivṛttaka*, and so forth; yet now, you take the twelve types such as the *Bhaiṣajyaguru* and *Vajra* [sūtras] as [the twelve divisions].

"The twelve divisions [of the canon]—this is an error upon an error. The current discussion of the fundamental texts places over seven thousand two hundred scrolls as the recitation for the beginning, with the *Fǎlún Bǎochàn* (Jeweled Repentance of the Dharma-Wheel) appended at the end; this serves as an introduction for future examinations of the canon."
If every word emits light, why worry that they will not gather? Did Māyā not say:
"When that wondrous radiance entered my body, although the dimensions of my physical form did not exceed its original state, it had in fact already transcended all worlds.
Why is this so? At that time, my body was equal in measure to empty space, capable of fully containing the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions."
Because I adorn the various palaces through my taking of birth, I am the mother of these Bodhisattvas who take birth in this world-system of four continents.
It is likewise throughout the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system, across ten billion sets of four continents, and within all Jambudvīpas.
Nevertheless, this body of mine is fundamentally non-dual; it does not abide in one place, nor does it abide in many places.
Question: The Tathāgata emits great radiance everywhere, and within each ray of light are immeasurable Buddhas.
Why is it that you do not expound the Yoga every day, but instead set forth this matter only on the seventh day, while for the preceding six days your spirit and mind appear somewhat lax?

Answer: The ritual grounds for water and land are fundamentally based on the laws of fasting (*upavāsa*). It is appropriate to integrate the six realms of existence as human and celestial beings, serving together in one assembly.
Regarding the partaking of food from the Triple Gem: offering food is but one branch of the great fast (*mahā-upavāsa*). One should focus the mind on the root and prune away the branches.

As for the reason why the seventh day must be extensively propagated, it is to send off the Sage and subsequently hold a final assembly to demonstrate the heart that never ceases in delivering sentient beings. There are those whose benefit from the inner altar has not yet been deep.

Alternatively, it may be possible to add further: after the two cycles of preaching the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* and the completion of the record of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, he further expounded the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*.

As the sutra says: "If there are sentient beings who see a bodhisattva practicing the path to enlightenment, whether they believe or doubt, the bodhisattva shall, through various mundane and supramundane skillful means, gather them in."
To act as their retinue and cause them to attain non-retrogression regarding *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*—this is the intended meaning.
Question: Sentient beings differ in their physical forms; their karmic actions and voices are likewise immeasurable. All such [beings]...
All these can be manifested through the majestic spiritual power of the *Sāgaramudrā-samādhi*.

As for this present painted scroll, since it approximates their number and further transforms all beings of the four evil destinies into the forms of humans and devas—is there anyone who can explain how this is so? Answer: When the Buddha enters sentient beings, he becomes entirely one with sentient beings;

when sentient beings enter the Buddha, they become entirely one with the Buddha. Thus, the form of the Buddha is identical to that of humans and devas, and humans and devas [are identical to the Buddha].
Only by assuming such a form can one receive offerings from humans and devas; it would surely be illogical to claim that one must sit in a body belonging to the evil realms within a *bodhimaṇḍa*.
As a sutra says: "In all places and among all classes of beings, I manifest in forms identical to theirs through skillful means.
Thus, one may know that when the ordinary and the sage intersect, their resonance must be mutual. How could one remain stuck in the shell of ignorance, deluded and self-enclosed?
I shall not follow the old path. This reduction in the number of dharma scrolls is not intended to be eccentric;
rather, I have observed that when too many scrolls are hung up, they tend to obscure one another. Now, I have fixed it so that there is exactly one scroll per seat, which ensures peace and stability.
Furthermore, within each individual scroll, the superior and inferior colors represent their respective ranks of honor;
thus, the eleven seats in the upper hall are each solemn and majestic, revealed in successive layers, for I dare not omit anything. This serves to assist the power of contemplation.
One must ensure that the initial cause is not mistaken. When the observer’s spirit is perfected, the holy and the ordinary dwell together.
Question: If Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and others did not appear in the world, there would be not a single sentient being capable of attaining peace and happiness.
Śākyamuni, our Original Teacher, was the most intimate to sentient beings; why then entrust them all exclusively to Vairocana?
To avoid being estranged from them: if this is indeed the case, how can Vairocana be said to benefit those with the five types of faculties?

For what reason does the teaching of the Perfect [Vehicle] specify that its intended audience consists only of bodhisattvas of the highest-highest capacity, ordinary beings, and non-Buddhists—while even those of the superior capacity are excluded?

Answer: The faculties have their stages of ripening; the teachings have their nuances of suppression and exaltation; the Dharmas have their partiality and completeness; and phenomena have their universality and limitation.
This present site of practice is the most excellent among the excellent. How could it be that our Buddha cannot merge the three bodies—Dharma, Reward, and Transformation—into one?
Moreover, have you not heard that from within the body of a single Buddha, he manifests as immeasurable Buddhas with the sound of thunder?
Pervading all lands, he expounds the Dharma as deep as the ocean.

Question: Regarding the phenomena perceived in the world, the mind alone is the master; according to its interpretations, one grasps various marks, which are inverted and not in accordance with reality.
Why then, at the time of bathing the Sage, do you give rise to the dualistic perception that discriminates between male and female?
Answer: There are two kinds of sages. First, those who are both noble in body and noble [in nature], such as the Three Jewels.

Second, those who are noble in nature despite having ordinary bodies, such as those manifested as Vajradeva and the leaders of the Eight Divisions. In today’s opening session, these two types of sages are clearly revealed.
We are all present at this Dharma assembly. The single matter of bathing is a necessity for sentient beings;

it is like a lamp illuminating the eyes or food pleasing the palate—things that must be sought according to the capacities and inclinations of ordinary people. To provide these things as an offering to the Sage is an act of filial piety.
How can one sever such ordinary sentiments and yet claim to be making an offering to the Sage? At that time, all sentient beings within that assembly, because they saw...

The Tathāgata has extinguished suffering and eliminated hindrances, and is thus capable of receiving the noble Dharma; therefore, his majestic deportment is not something to be confused with or established in vain.
Without destroying the characteristics of the world, he fulfills his heart of great compassion.
Question: All dharma-gates are an inexhaustible ocean, yet they converge within the single dharma-dharmapāṭha.

Why is it that the present meal for the saṃgha is not considered a true "feeding"? Answer: Feeding the saṃgha is an extraordinary and great undertaking; even one such occasion is not easy to achieve, let alone three.
During the seven days, the spirit may not be able to remain focused on the outflow-free (anāsrava) state. Therefore, money is used as a substitute.
Offering rice serves to manifest this mind; compared to a hasty meal, it is ten times more composed. As the Sūtra says:
"All the marks of the Buddha’s body manifest immeasurable Buddhas. Since the Buddha’s body is thus, his enlightened activities are likewise so.
With a mind of liberation, one makes offerings to the Arhats; there is no need to give rise again to thoughts of attachment.

Furthermore, regarding those matters you have not yet asked about, I shall follow them up with my own discourse; I do not dare to conform to convention out of mere expediency, nor do I claim to delight in eccentricity.

First, the primary principle is that while the donor’s initial resolve may differ, one must ensure that the measure of the Tathāgata remains uniform. Second, it is different that no separate table for the host of the feast is established;
this is so that the minds of all sentient beings may be made identical. Third, there is no cause for disdaining a large number of people being formally delivered across [to liberation].

1. While the ritual implements may differ, one must ensure that the objects of liberation are identical. 2. While the four presiding masters may differ in their dietary habits—whether frugal or refined—one must ensure that the principle of resonance and response is identical.
3. While the ritual tablets need not be divided into separate sets, one must ensure that the essence of the great vows is identical.

4. While the number of administrative officers need not be excessive, one must ensure that their pure mindfulness is identical. 5. While the outer altar need not necessarily consist of twenty-four [sections].

1. Although the people differ, one must ensure their reverent faith is identical. 2. Although the affairs of the inner altar often involve night practices, one must ensure the engagement of the six sense faculties is identical. 3.
Although there are differences in the increase or decrease of musical instruments on the inner altar, one must ensure the sounds are identical by day and night. 4.

Although there are differences in generosity regarding the lack of pride in possessing much wealth, one must ensure the cause for seeking deliverance is identical. The Master of the Dharma must personally resolve his mind with compassion.
This is the Perfection of Crossing Over (*pāramitā*). Only when one’s fundamental mind-body becomes identical with that of all Tathāgatas can it be compared to being invited with white gold;
otherwise, how does it differ from an ordinary ritual site? I fear there would be little resonance or transformation.

Since the *zhāi* (fasting/retreat) has no presiding host, all sentient beings are simultaneously both host and guest. One should temporarily set up a single mat beside the presiding Dharma-master and invite those from both the upper and lower halls.
Select one person to respond to each inquiry; it requires only those with sincere intent.
If the positions are fixed and the host and guest stand apart, the performance of the ritual may conversely fail to reach the divine. This is the twenty-fourth seat, the pivot of the correct measure:
a thousand or ten hundred people share one tablet, and ten tablets occupy one position; there is no need to take great expense as a virtue, for it might conversely lead to [negligence].
Those to be saved are few and far between. One must ensure that all people are able to exert themselves so as to deliver their own parents; only then will there be no cause for regret.
As for those who do not believe and enter, there is nothing that can be done. The moment a thought arises, one has already entered this Dharma-realm.
It costs only one hundred coins per person; since those who come find it easy, its practice is not difficult. May the Dharma of the Tathāgata long abide.
The exquisite offerings from both the upper and lower halls are presented to be enjoyed by the great assembly, while the presiding master represents the recitation of mantras.
One must not eat [the offerings] with relish; instead, prepare them simply and coarsely, taking only what is sufficient. Make it a priority to communicate with a refined and sincere mind.

If the ritual recitation (*biaobai*) is too polished, it becomes overly specialized; when one is preoccupied with such specialization, the benefit to sentient beings is shallow. One need not restrict oneself to whether the style is refined or plain.
For temporary purposes, one may employ those who have a slight knowledge of the texts; the ritual does not seek aesthetic perfection.

One should appoint many officiants, as it is merely for the purpose of distributing expenses. It would be excellent if twenty-four people could perform the outer altar rites, but otherwise, twelve positions will suffice.
Even with twelve people, it is permissible to leave three or five positions vacant; however, the number of positions must remain twelve.
This was so that the sacred relics could be conveyed to the twenty-four altars for temporary stationing:
from the west, altars one through six correspond to altars twelve through thirteen; from the east, altars six through one correspond to altars one through twelve.

The altars borrow their positions for a brief period to allow all humans and devas to pay their respects. From the third, fourth, and fifth watches of the night, the winter nights are sufficient [for this].
By means of gathering these matters, after sunrise the gates and fences are locked; people are permitted to pay their respects and view the site from outside the fence.

Thus, both movement and stillness are realized as the Dharma-realm. The clamor of drums and cymbals is no match for gold and jade swaying in the wind, which is further complemented by a pair of bells.

The balance between the sparse and the dense is thus achieved. Since one does not seek excessive gold from the host of the vegetarian feast (*zhāizhǔ*), arrogance is once and for all eliminated, and a heart of reverence shines forth clearly;
this is the Three Jewels emitting light.
The former guest asked again, "Can Yijie know this in advance? He replied, "Why not?

Once the Dharma Master had formed this intention, two days prior [to the event], he inquired whether the matters for both the inner and outer altars were complete. Thereupon, he retired to a single room and performed the *shixiang chanhui* (repentance of the true mark) for all sentient beings of the *dharmadhātu*.
On the day before, the Dharma Master personally inspected the plaques and scrolls and installed them everywhere.
[They] do not perform the rites. After noon, the small bells and drums are struck at the inner altar, and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-kṣānti* text is recited once.

On the first day: at the third watch, the outer altar is sprinkled with pure water; at the fourth watch, the boundary is established at the inner altar; at the fifth watch, messengers are dispatched to plant the banners.
On the second day: at the fourth watch, the assembly is invited to the hall; at the fifth watch, the ritual bathing is performed. On the third day: at the fourth watch.
The offering for the Upper Hall. At the fifth watch, the request for the amnesty. On this day at the noon hour, all monks both inside and outside the monastery take money in place of their meal.
On the fourth day, at the third watch, the request for the descent from the hall. At the fourth watch, the offering of the bath. At the fifth watch, the recitation of the precepts.

On the fifth day, at the fourth watch, the recitation of the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind). At the fifth watch, the offering for the descent from the hall. On this day at the noon hour, the feeding of the monks.

As in the aforementioned ritual: on the sixth day, during the fourth watch, the presiding master and his attendants perform the incense offering in both the upper and lower halls, sincerely proclaiming their earnest petitions.

At the hour of Si (10–11 am), they carry out the rite of releasing living beings. At the hour of Wei (1–3 pm), they provide fodder for the sacrificial animals. On the seventh day, during the fifth watch, they make universal offerings in both the upper and lower halls.

At the hour of Si (10–11 am), they conclude the vows. At noon, they provide a vegetarian feast for the monks as prescribed above. At the hour of Wei (1–3 pm), they welcome [the deities] to the outer altar. At the hour of Shen (5–7 pm) [the ritual continues].
At that time, the Sage was escorted [to the altar]. At the hour of Xu (7–9 p.m.), the assembly performed the yoga of *bali* offerings. It concluded at the hour of Hai (9–11 p.m.).
On the following day, the presiding master received those from the outer altar—both humans and devas—and revealed to them the principle that the Dharma-realm has neither beginning nor end.
Supplementary Discussion: That which is venerated is the spiritual luminosity of the Triple Gem and sentient beings. That upon which this spirituality relies is...
The banners, plaques, and painted scrolls are all manifestations of the heart-light of the presiding Dharma-master.
However, if one constructs approximately ten characters on a single plaque to encompass both the general and specific characteristics, then all ten plaques would be identical.

Only in the twenty-fourth case—where each individual plaque is inscribed with hundreds or thousands of different names—are the plaques distinct. In the twenty-fifth section, there is a difference based on the specific seating arrangement. As for the preceding...

Twenty-three. These must not differ in the slightest; this is a state of peace of mind and rational attainment (the wording used when requesting [the tablets] shall serve as the model for the style of the tablets).
All tablets have a jeweled canopy (*ratnacchattra*) painted at the top and a lotus flower painted at the bottom. The center is made of yellow paper; for those in the lower hall, red paper is used.

The messengers (*shi*) also use red paper (ten tablets for the messengers constitute one position, combining the Celestial Path, the Earthly Path, and the Earthly Court into one). For the fourth seat, no title is used.

The Tiantai school values excellence and praises the "Two Flowers" (Huayan). It abandons the person to focus on the Dharma, thereby enabling communication across other lands. [In the ritual procedures,] the eleventh, twenty-fourth, and twenty-fifth [days] do not communicate [with others].

Within the "Universal" (pǔ), one concentrates the mind; within the "Total" (zǒng), there are distinct characteristics (*bèxiàng*). (The *shūshǐ* and *shèshǐ* [invocation slips] differ in their phrasing and do not follow one another.

Offerings are made to the upper hall and the lower hall. They form a single vow together, each possessing its own significance. Invitations and the three offerings are interspersed with the chanting of names. The primary attendants occupy two seats; the total and the individual are the same.
These are distinct. Thus, one transcribes the numinous mind of the Dharma-realm. Regarding the five vegetables and five fruits, prepare them as a single bowl;
offer fresh flowers, fruit, incense, and ointments on a plate, along with small snacks for the Dharma. If one can truly achieve spiritual transformation, why need there be such excessive fuss?
Aside from the three offerings, one should offer morning gruel and midday rice for seven days with incense and lamps; these are not to be omitted.

One should also sprinkle water for purification at the outer altar and circumambulate the inner altar once, to demonstrate the mutual interpenetration of the multilayered Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

It is best to perform the *Ratna-sādhana* (Precious Repentance) with a composed and respectful demeanor; it must not be hurried. On the seventh day, one must certainly prostrate during the hour of the Snake (*yīshí*).

[Recite] the "Chapter on the Vows of Practice" (Pranidhāna-paṭala) to conclude [the recitation]. (For those who recite the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, they should join in the recitation; thus the Avataṃsaka recitation is also completed at this time. Then, continue with the Buddhas.
Thus, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha enter into that mindfulness together. When bathing [the image], burn paper [silk] strips; for each seat, there are ten bundles.

At the time of offering, the first two have none, while the last one has them, prepared for the purpose of sending off [the deceased] (in total, five hundred pieces). Use three colors, or combine blue and black;
they are three feet wide and nine inches long. Stack the papers to form rolls, using high-quality red paper and silver.
Folded strips are used to bind them together. When rolling them up, recite the *Cīvara-mantra*.
Sincerity can transform these into offerings. For the Pure Path, do not use the name "Immortal Bridge"; for honoring the Sages, do not use the tune of the "Immortal Crossing the Street.

This is to ensure that sentient beings have no deluded thoughts. One tablet and one offering petition constitute one bundle; ten bundles are tied together with paper and silk. Add another layer of paper wrapping.

Bind it. Use precious jewels as an accessory (these are paper jewels; they are used during the offering and represent the Dharma-jewel of the scripture scrolls). For the twenty-fifth seat, do not use a tray;
after the rite is completed, it may be dissolved within the lattice. There are twenty-four oil lamps in total, both for the cauldrons and the upright lamps.
Outside the inner altar gate, cover them all with cloth canopies, lined with oil-paper, and install wooden railings below within the lattice.
Thus, the wooden awning is free of leaks. Alongside the three purified paths, stands are erected for hanging lamps, incense burners, and banners.
These are also used by the presiding ritual master for sprinkling purification water and for bathing in the upper and lower halls.
Within the inner altar, there is one large and ten small cups for pure water; these are divided into large and small sizes to await various uses. Only in the center of the inner altar...
Hang four lamps from the single partition; [display] four long banners, one lapis lazuli [vessel], one *huānmén* (joy-gate), and four *púduōn* (lotus-pads).
The circular altar consists of lamps, mirrors, banners, flowers, and other items. The six types of offering lists are: incense, flowers, ointments, precious objects, food, and fruit.
Two cups are for tea and rice; one bowl is for vegetables; one incense burner and two stands; and gold coins, paper, and silk.

Do not use undergarments. As for the materials of robes that share the same characteristics and the forms of robes that differ in appearance, these are distributed between paper-silk and painted scrolls.
It is unnecessary to manufacture actual garments, such as necklaces, crowns, robes, sashes, armor, or helmets;

for across the sacred and the mundane, ancient and modern, male and female, principal and attendant, civil and military, monastic and lay, the differences are extreme, and one must not seek them by "marking the boat" [after the water has flowed away]. Bathing...

When offering silk garments, one must insert three branches of *tōge* (Chinese roses) into each bundle; this applies to all such bundles. These flowers should all be small red ones (one thousand branches being required).
Furthermore, for the offerings of invitation, bathing, and worship, as well as for the attendants and the presiding judge, these same flowers are used (requiring another one thousand branches).
As for the seating arrangements, they may be determined and set out on the following day, provided that the power of Great Compassion is sufficient.
At the *Dōjō*, one may take the most essential points of the *Zhengdu* (Correct Deliverance) and record them upon the attendant tablets (*baishi*). Incense should be burned over them daily.
When there are offerings for the terrestrial and aquatic realms (*shuilu*), these tablets should be used as attendants; thus, the true spirits will surely attain unimpeded penetration.

Request twenty tablets for the Officials—formerly called *Fuguan* (Officer of Talismans), now called *Shizhe* (Messenger)—divided between the upper and lower halls with ten tablets each. Request twenty tablets for the Judging Officials (*Panguan*). [Request] twenty tablets for the Pardons (*She*).

There are ten official tablets; both the general and specific ones are inscribed together in the same format, using ten to symbolize the inexhaustible. Paper images and paper horses are not used at all.
Facing the altar for the offering of food (*śrāddha*), one provides offerings to the Great Being Mañjuśrī and the *śmaśāna* (charnel ground) scroll.
To the left and right, respectively, one lights a lamp of compassion. In front of the outer altar, a canopy is prepared, and a reed mat is placed over the water jar.
Prepare oil-paper on the tray; it may be omitted when the weather is clear. Substitute money for the monks' meal:
thirty-six units constitute one *zhāi* (fast-offering), and twelve units constitute one *qīn* (offering); this represents the forty-eight vows of aspiration. On the day of the fast, at exactly noon.
One person shall wear monastic robes and provide offerings at the gate. It would be appropriate to present these offerings at midday when ascending the hall;

however, fearing that the atmosphere may become too boisterous, it is better to do so during the divine stillness of the night. After descending from the hall, one does not eat until after mid-afternoon.

Having received the Bodhisattva precepts, they are regarded as equal to sons of the Buddha; thus, one cannot bear to treat them as if they were of the evil realms. Throughout the six periods of day and night, incense is burned.

Sound the chimes. Do not allow confusion (if it is an offering, avoid the hour of Yín; if it is a send-off, avoid the hour of Shēn). For the inner altar, employ the essential meaning; for the outer altar, affix the written notice.

The number of memorial tablets offered corresponds to the number of [deceased] individuals. As for the funds for releasing living beings (*fangsheng*) and the funds for sacrificial grain, starting from ten thousand coins and increasing up to ten or even a hundred times that amount is also permissible.
Regarding the monks’ feast, the funds for releasing living beings and the sacrificial grain are all placed upon the general offerings (*pusong*).

After striking the chime (*qing*), one performs a single prostration before the incense and lamps, then removes them and places them outside the enclosure at the main gate of the feast hall. This concludes the section on releasing living beings and the sacrificial grain.

Exit through the left and right gates. The living beings released are placed outside the enclosure. The presiding Dharma Master recites the Three Refuges within the enclosure, while two persons inside the enclosure receive them on his behalf.

Generally, the Sūtra treasury does not rely on haste; for seven days prior, select conscientious individuals from the ten directions to oversee and recite the texts in their respective locations, recording the scriptural evidence clearly and dedicating the merit back to the altar. You should know this.
This assembly does not limit itself to any particular direction; its arrangement and its perfect fusion are equally unimpeded.
It unites the movements of heaven and earth, and the realms of the underworld, within a single station. Only when one descends from the hall can one attain such clarity and resonance.

Whether there or here, the spirits and deities exercise their powers. This is the general amnesty edict. Beyond the ten directions, one adds the center; this is the sovereign of the fundamental world.
The purport of this manuscript concerns the Dharma-realm of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra and the Sahā world-system. Within one of the four continents, specifically Jambudvīpa in the south,
at the Kukkutārāma monastery in the eastern land, upon the inner altar by water and land, I, the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu [Name], respectfully—
With this intent, I humbly address the Three Jewels of the inner altar above, all the holy deities, and the seats of the infinite true spirits.
I prostrate myself, for that which is pure and fundamental is nothing other than liberation; the wondrously luminous true limit is entirely endowed with majestic spiritual power.
It is fundamentally a state of mutual interpenetration and perfect penetration; how could it be biased toward light or darkness, form or emptiness? Alas, how is it that such a sudden...

Unaware, they lose the true suchness (tathatā) and wander in confusion through the ten gates of manifestation and concealment—where phenomena and principle (dharma-lakṣaṇa/tattva) are established, revealed, or eclipsed.

They are inverted regarding the six characteristics (ṣaḍ-lakṣaṇa): the general and the particular, the same and the different, and formation and disintegration. Thus, they grasp the coarse while neglecting the subtle, like mistaking a veil for the head itself.
Vast and boundless is the expanse of kalpas; circling through birth and death, the infinite and intense sufferings are truly pitiable.
Surveying the four evil realms, one sees immeasurable sentient beings sinking and drowning in succession, finding no stable footing.

Even if they should temporarily dwell among humans or devas, receiving retribution according to conditions, they continue to create karma amidst suffering and soon sink back once more. Even if there are those who practice cultivation, for the most part...
Lacking right view, they follow the faction of false teachers and companions; incited and deluded, they mistakenly enter the snares of Māra and ultimately sink into the cycle of birth and death.

Some have long cultivated great power, yet when confronted by the majestic and extraordinary spirits of the heavens, their habitual tendencies remain so firm that they do not know how to return [to the source].

Others are intelligent, refined, and endowed with wealth, honor, and auspiciousness; yet by craving these minor pleasures, they all return to great suffering. There is none who does not [suffer thus].

To harbor gratitude while nursing resentment brings forth poison and invites calamity; it leads to failure in one's affairs and injury to one's life, turning one’s back on the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

Furthermore, there are those who forget their original vows, whose minds become deluded by external objects, and who regress to the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*), willingly following the ways of Māras and heretics.

At the extreme, some manifest the appearance of a Bodhisattva while harboring the heart of a *yakṣa*, destroying the Dharma and the Sangha—neither Māra nor Buddha. Such misfortunes afflict sentient beings.

Upon what does consciousness rely? Alas for the pitiable masses who, in the face of the True Doctrine, remain ignorant of it. Therefore, I propagate the orthodox teaching and hereby inaugurate the True Altar.
Unifying those of the water, land, and empty space, I deliver the boundless; merging the immortals, the Confucian scholars, and the sons of the Buddha, I melt them all into a single boundary.
Together with my new kinsmen from countless lifetimes, we come as one to this Great Assembly of Universal Radiance.
The flavor of the Dharma nourishes the spirit; wondrous sounds awaken the mind. Having attained such composure and transformation, they subsequently move in circumambulation as a protective retinue.
Relying on this single truth, they mysteriously penetrate the Dharma-realm. The radiance of the Dragon Treasury deeply embraces the net of precious vows;
within the Flower Adornment Sea of Lands, the body of Amitābha manifests perfectly. May I attain the skillful means of the hand and vow to deliver sentient beings without ceasing.
Obstructed. The Buddha’s grace is swift and efficacious; it fulfills my heart’s aspirations. I hereby manifest my utmost sincerity and pray for your compassionate empowerment.
On this day, month, and year, the bhikṣu [Name] respectfully submits.
Preface (with the four characters "Water and Land Preface" added at the beginning): We have heard that the single truth flows forth, embodying the causes of both sentient beings and Buddhas;
the myriad dharmas are perfect and eternal, manifesting the function of liberation and compassion. Wherever the capacities of beings lie, assemblies of the Dharma arise.
Now, within the Dharmadhātu of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, in this Sahā world-system, under one set of four continents, in the southern continent of Jambudvīpa...

At the Chicken Garden in the Eastern Land, Bodhisattva Bhikṣus such as [Name] and others, for the purpose of inaugurating a *dharmadhātu* (place of practice) for the universal benefit of both the holy and the mundane,

now rely upon the fourfold assembly of disciples who, in accordance with their service to the Buddha and cultivation of causes, pray for the fulfillment of their aspirations. With bodies purified by bathing and incense burning,

they reverently take refuge in the eternal, omnipresent, and immeasurable Triple Gem of the ten directions, and the Great Assembly of Beings Aqueous and Terrestrial, including those in the netherworld.
May the Sages and ordinary beings alike extend their compassionate radiance to bear witness to this humble sincerity.

We humbly submit that, from the [day], [month], and [year] of this present year, we respectfully establish this ritual arena in accordance with the True Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), continuing until the [day] when it is completed.
Within this period, having consulted the various liturgical manuals, we single-mindedly invoke the Fourfold Assembly of the ten directions and the entire Dharma-realm.
The six classes of ordinary beings and the myriad virtues and spirits descend in splendor upon this Dharma assembly.

Relying upon the fourfold assembly, we shall, on the appointed day, recite the Dragon Canon—the immeasurable numinous texts of the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna sūtras, vinayas, śāstras, and dhāraṇīs—totaling seven thousand two hundred and eighty fascicles (including those exceeding this number).
We shall prostrate before the Jewel Repentance of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and concurrently perform the rites of food-bestowal, the liberation of living beings, and the vegetarian fast.

The monastic community performed various dharma services including the recitation of the Buddha’s name. They prepared twenty-odd seating arrangements for the pure vegetarian feast of tea, cakes, and seasonal fruits, as well as a grand universal offering assembly.
Gold, silver, and silk fabrics were distributed in full measure according to each seat. All these offerings were combined to accumulate merit.
Together we extend this dedication to the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and to the devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits.

Next, may it further pervade universally throughout all worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, benefiting both enemies and kin equally, and providing sustenance for all who have shown us kindness. May my deep vows be fully repaid and fulfilled without fail;

may all others from the ten directions be entirely gathered in, and may all be simultaneously rescued. I look up with hope that the Three Honored Ones will eternally witness this, and that the myriad sages will shed their radiance, so that this great [merit]...
Opening the gate of salvation and benefit, this is a great festival of universal liberation. May every being be freed from obstacles, and may every realm merge into emptiness.
May we forever receive the illumination of the Sun of Wisdom and be equally protected by the Clouds of Dharma.

Based upon the petitions of the fourfold assembly at this altar, it is appropriate to issue this public notice. This notice must be issued (add "so that both the hidden and the manifest may all know" here). Issued as a notice on the [day], [month], and [year].
Preface to the Commentary: I have heard that the true source is not partitioned, and the precious nature is perfectly encompassing.

It unites the minds of all sentient beings and all Buddhas, manifesting the wondrousness of the single ultimate and the boundless. Deeply and profoundly they appear together; closely and secretly they are all illuminated.

Now, within this Flower Adornment Dharma-realm, in this Sahā world-system, under one set of four continents, in Jambudvīpa in the south, specifically at the Cock Garden (Kukkuṭārāma) in the land of the East.
The Dharma assembly has been inaugurated for the universal benefit of both the holy and the mundane. To bring this gathering to full completion, we submit this memorial for your perusal.

We, the disciples of the fourfold assembly, having undertaken the offering of vegetarian feasts in service to the Buddha to pray for the fulfillment of our aspirations, now bathe ourselves, burn incense, and with solemn reverence take refuge in the eternal, omnipresent Triple Gem of the ten directions, as well as all the holy and mundane beings, both hidden and manifest, of the Great Assembly for Beings of Water and Land. Together we perform [this rite].
Compassionate Light, please bear witness to my humble sincerity. I prostrate myself; (herein I express my earnest intent in no more than one hundred characters).

Beginning from this day, the [day/month/year] of the current year, I shall establish a *dharmadhātu* (sacred precinct), concluding on the [specific] day. Within this period, I shall consult and adapt the ritual protocols.

With single-minded devotion, we extend our invitation to all within the ten directions and the Dharma-realm—the four classes of noble beings and the six realms of ordinary beings, and all spirits endowed with myriad virtues—to descend in person upon this Dharma assembly.
Relying upon the fourfold assembly, we shall, on the appointed day prior to the ceremony, recite the entire Dragon Canon:

the immeasurable sacred texts of the various Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna divisions, including the Sūtras, Vinayas, Śāstras, and Dhāraṇīs, totaling seven thousand two hundred and eighty fascicles. We also pay homage to the *Dharmacakra-ratna-kṣamaṇa* (The Jewel Repentance of the Turning of the Wheel of Dharma).
Simultaneously, we distribute food and release living beings, provide meals for the Sangha, recite the Buddha’s name, and perform various Dharma services.

We prepare pure vegetarian feasts with tea, seasonal fruits, and delicacies for over twenty seats, all as part of a grand universal offering. Gold, silver, and silk fabrics are distributed in full measure according to each seat.
May the merit gathered from these offerings be dedicated together to the Triple Gem of the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, and to the devas, nāgas, and spirits.
Next, the fragrance spread universally, pervading the entire realm of *sāhasra-lokadhātus*. It benefited both enemies and kin equally, providing sustenance to all who were indebted.

As the spiritual causes were fulfilled, the precious moisture of the Dharma-light was opened for all; the sublime assembly was vast and profound, and the great celebration of the Dharma feast was successfully accomplished.

The Three Honored Ones reflect like mirrors; the successive sages are linked like pearls. They are tranquil, containing the moon within the water yet not being empty; they wondrously manifest as clouds of lamps yet are not obstructed.
Object and mind penetrate one another; body and realm are transparent and clear. They sweep away the lingering darkness of fine gauze and purify the subtle obstructions of every pore.
May they graciously grant their response and forever protect all sentient beings. On this day, month, and year, we reverently offer to the Buddha.

Requesting the transcription of the Flower Garland Dharma-realm, the Sahā world-system, one set of four continents, and Jambudvīpa in the southern quarter.
